newsitem.title: ITALY: Fireman who saved shroud hailed as hero of fire.
newsitem.headline: Fireman who saved shroud hailed as hero of fire.

text.p: Turin's Cardinal Giovanni Saldarini proclaimed the rescue of the Turin Shroud from a blaze on Saturday as a miracle but its survival owed at least as much to the courage and presence of mind of an Italian fireman.

As flames engulfed a cathedral chapel in this northwestern city in the early hours of Saturday morning, Mario Trematore smashed his way through a bullet-proof shield to snatch the silver casket storing the winding sheet to safety.

Trematore, who was later treated in hospital for cuts and bruises, gave a dramatic account of how he saved the burial cloth from almost certain destruction in an interview carried in a special edition of Turin daily La Stampa.

"I found the strength in that symbol, the symbol of the shroud. Just think that glass can withstand bullets but I managed somehow to break it all the same. It's almost a miracle," said the 44-year-old Trematore.

The mysterious shroud, which bears the ghostly imprint of a man, is revered by many Roman Catholics as Christ's burial cloth although scientists dispute its authenticity and say it only dates back to the middle ages.

Trematore said the impulse to risk life and limb to save the rectangular casket came to him when he realised the Guarini chapel, built in the 17th century as a permanent home for the cloth, appeared to be on the verge of collapse.
"All appeared to be lost. Pieces of the Guarini chapel were crashing down and there was a serious danger that it would bury everything -- the casket, the altar and all of us," he said.
Trematore was one of a team of 140 firemen rushed in to fight the blaze from as far away as Milan, 120 km (75 miles) away.

A large crowd had gathered outside the Renaissance cathedral in the heart of the city to watch the dramatic inferno, which shot flames up into the night sky and started to spread to the adjoining palace.
"Then I hurled myself through the flames with a hammer and I was able to save the shroud. There was nothing else to do at that point. We were about to lose it forever," he said.
Trematore grabbed the silver box with both hands and ran out of the chapel, blood streaming down his face, and was met by a group of priests who were weeping uncontrollably.
"I don't know who they were. They were nearly all crying. Even I was, probably," he said.
Police took the casket from Trematore and as they carried it triumphantly down the cathedral nave and out into the open a loud cheer went up among the crowd of onlookers.
A police car sped off with the casket to take it to Cardinal Saldarini's residence for safe keeping.
"We are practically certain that the shroud did not suffer any damage," Turin's Fire Chief Michele Ferraro told Reuters. "We do not think any water could have seeped into the box."
